extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in the nature of scientific practice and paradigms
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the criteria and conceptual standards Kuhn uses to characterize 'normal science', its problems, rules, and the role of paradigms in guiding research; aimed at readers studying scientific method and history of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of normal scientific problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal scientific work is largely composed of three classes of problems: determination of significant fact, matching of facts with theory, and articulation (clarification and reformulation) of theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn states these three classes 'exhaust, I think, the literature of normal science, both empirical and theoretical.' Examples: Coulomb's designing apparatus (theory-informed construction) and experiments to distinguish heating-by-compression theories (same people constructing both theories and tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of normal science (expectation-limited results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science problems typically do not aim to produce major conceptual or phenomenal novelties; expected outcomes lie within a narrow, assimilable range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects whose outcomes fall outside the anticipated (paradigm-consistent) range are usually judged research failures; routine repetition is often spurned because what matters is solving the puzzle, not discovering intrinsically novel results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzle-characteristics of normal-science problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that qualify as scientific puzzles must have an assured existence of a solution and rules that limit acceptable solutions and solution procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn compares to jigsaw and crossword puzzles: intrinsic interest isn't required, but solvability and prescribed constraints (e.g., use all pieces, interlock without forcing) are. The community's paradigm provides analogous rules and assurances of solvability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to relate empirical results to theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental measurements must be shown, in terms of the established body of theory, to produce the quantities that theory recognizes; otherwise they may be considered meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: wavelength apparatus must be analyzed so its numbers enter theory as wave lengths; electron-scattering maxima were meaningless until related to wave-like behavior of matter and apparatus redesigned to correlate unequivocally with theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible solutions constrained by established laws and theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing laws and theoretical generalizations set puzzles and bound acceptable solutions; proposals that violate those laws change the paradigm rather than solve the puzzle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton’s laws governed eighteenth- and nineteenth-century problems; attempts to deviate from the inverse square law would redefine the puzzle instead of solving the established one. Laws/theories thus function as problem-setting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental commitments as rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Commitments to preferred types of instruments and to legitimate modes of using them operate as rules within a tradition and constrain acceptable research practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: changing attitudes toward fire in chemical analysis; physiologists' resistance to physical experimentation (Helmholtz); the history of chromatography showing endurance of instrumental commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi‑metaphysical (ontological/methodological) commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Longstanding, high-level commitments about the nature of entities and acceptable forms of explanation (e.g., corpuscularism) shape both what counts as explanation and which problems are pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corpuscularism after Descartes dictated that phenomena be explained by shape, size, motion, and interaction of corpuscles; this both limited ontology and prescribed methodological reduction to corpuscular action, guiding problem choice (e.g., transmutation reactions in chemistry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-level commitments of scientific practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists share broader commitments: to understand the world, to extend the precision and scope of existing orderings, to scrutinize nature in empirical detail, and to refine techniques or theories when disorder appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These commitments are less concrete than laws or instruments but are necessary characteristics without which 'no man is a scientist' and they guide the overall aims and style of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms as repositories of exemplars and models (priority over explicit rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared paradigms—textbook examples, lectures, laboratory exercises—serve as the primary guide for research practice; rules may be abstracted from them but paradigms can operate without a fully articulated set of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes that paradigms are learned through exposure to exemplars and applications; historians can identify paradigms more easily than a definitive set of rules. Paradigms can guide research even when practitioners cannot state underlying abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit knowledge and learning by application
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific education transmits concepts, laws, and techniques primarily through concrete applications and practice; much of what guides practitioners is tacit, learned through doing rather than explicit rule formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students learn meanings of terms like 'force' or 'mass' by applying them in problem solving and laboratory practice; success in research often manifests this tacit knowledge rather than explicit theoretical articulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem selection constrained by paradigm (assured-solvability criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific communities select and encourage problems that, given the paradigm, can be assumed to have solutions; problems not reducible to the puzzle form are often rejected as metaphysical or not scientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigms can insulate communities from socially important but non-reducible problems. This selection accelerates progress by focusing effort on problems only the community's lack of ingenuity should prevent solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of debate during pre-paradigm and revolutionary periods
rubrics_metrics.description: When paradigms are insecure or absent (pre-paradigm periods) or under attack (revolutions), disputes over legitimate methods, problems, and standards of solution proliferate; in stable paradigms such debates are largely absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn cites historical episodes (optics, electricity, chemistry, geology, quantum mechanics) where methodological debates mark transitions; while paradigms remain secure, rules and rationalizations are less salient to practitioners.
